faq.a: Contribution margin is price minus variable cost per unit. It is the amount each unit sold contributes toward covering fixed costs and then toward profit. In the worked example, a $50 price minus a $30 variable cost gives a $20 margin.

Break-even units equal fixed costs plus your profit target, divided by contribution margin. With no profit target, it is fixed costs divided by contribution margin. Break-even revenue is break-even units times price.
faq.q: How is the break-even point worked out?

faq.a: Add a profit target to see how many units you must sell to earn that profit, not just to cover costs. With $10,000 fixed costs, a $50 price, and a $30 variable cost, a $2,000 profit target raises break-even from 500 units to 600 units.

Yes, if variable cost per unit is equal to or higher than price, the margin is zero or negative and you lose money on every sale, so there is no break-even point. Raise the price or cut the variable cost first.
faq.q: What if my variable cost is higher than my price?

whenNotToUse: It assumes fixed costs, price, and variable cost per unit stay the same at every sales level. Real costs and prices often change with volume.
It does not include taxes, loan payments, or one-off costs, so it is a planning estimate, not a full profit forecast.
This is the general business break-even. ToolVerse also has a mortgage refinance break-even calculator and a relocation break-even calculator for those specific uses.
